section_title: Why did the midwives refuse Pharaoh’s command?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt. 9 “Look,” he said to his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us. 10 Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more; and if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.”

11 So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. As a result, they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh. 12 But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites. 13 They worked the Israelites ruthlessly 14 and made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields. Every service they imposed was harsh.

15 Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah, 16 “When you help the Hebrew women give birth, observe them on the birthstools. If the child is a son, kill him; but if it is a daughter, let her live.” 17 The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live. 18 So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?” 19 The midwives answered Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives.”

20 So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. 21 And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own. 22 Then Pharaoh commanded all his people: “Every son born to the Hebrews you must throw into the Nile, but every daughter you may allow to live.”

context_lines: A new king who does not know Joseph sees Israel’s growing population as a threat. He fears that they might join an enemy during war and leave Egypt. Forced labor is his first response: the Israelites build store cities, make bricks and work in the fields under harsh conditions.

The oppression does not achieve its purpose. The people continue to multiply, and Egyptian fear grows. Pharaoh then orders the midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill Hebrew boys at birth while letting the girls live.

The women fear God and let the boys live. The Hebrew verb can include reverence and honor, as [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/3372.htm) explains under its entry for fearing God, including these verses. Their reverence has a practical result: they refuse the king’s command to kill.

When questioned, they tell Pharaoh that Hebrew women give birth before a midwife arrives. God is good to the midwives, and the people keep growing. The BSB describes God giving the women families of their own. Pharaoh then extends the command to all his people: Hebrew boys are to be thrown into the Nile. The chapter ends with the threat that will surround Moses’ birth.
common_interpretation_lines: The main readings commend the women’s fear of God and their protection of the boys. Their reply to Pharaoh receives different explanations. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) sees no reason to doubt that the women were telling the truth about the births. [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/1.htm) understands the reply as a falsehood, while distinguishing God’s approval of their reverence and mercy from approval of the lie.

Catholic teaching in [Catechism 2482–2485](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_three/section_two/chapter_two/article_8/iii_offenses_against_truth.html) defines lying as intentional deception through falsehood and condemns it. That is a general teaching about truthfulness; those paragraphs do not decide whether the midwives’ particular reply was false.

The women’s identity is also read differently. Calvin takes them as Hebrew women. Wesley understands them as midwives serving the Hebrews who may themselves have been Egyptian. Both identify their fear of God as the reason they resist Pharaoh.

There is a further difference over the households in verse 21. The BSB and Wesley understand the blessing as families given to the midwives. Calvin applies the building of households to the growing families of Israel. Each reading connects the result with God preserving life through the women’s actions.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 7:18–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/7.htm) places this oppression immediately before Moses’ birth and upbringing. The threatened people are the people from whom God is preparing a deliverer. [Hebrews 11:23](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/11.htm) also remembers Moses’ parents acting in faith despite the king’s edict.

A later parallel appears in [Matthew 2:13–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/2.htm): another ruler orders the killing of boys, while God provides a way for Jesus to be preserved. This is a parallel in the threat and rescue, rather than a claim that the two accounts are identical in every detail.

The women’s choice also recalls the apostles’ response to an order to stop their witness in [Acts 5:27–29](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/5.htm). Obedience to God takes precedence when a human command directly opposes Him. The larger story shows God preserving His purpose through people whose faithfulness may look small beside royal power.
